Q: How to detect game cards in image? A:

I do not know if this helps, but this approach works for both your images in Python OpenCV.

  • Read the input (choose one of the two images)

  • Apply median filtering to smooth the background

  • Threshold on the white of the cards using cv2.inRange()

  • Apply morphology close to remove black regions inside those cards especially for those regions that touch the borders

  • Get external contours

  • For each contour:

    • Get the contour area

    • Filter out small extraneous regions

    • Get the bounding box

    • Filter out horizontal regions since the cards are more vertical than horizontal

    • Draw the contours as blue on a copy of the input

  • Save the images

Input images:

Image 1:

Image 2:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# choose the input name
name = "game_cards1"
# or
#name = "game_cards2"

# set filename
filename = name + ".jpg"

# read whichever image
img = cv2.imread(filename)

# get img shape
hh, ww = img.shape[:2]

# apply median filter to image to smooth background
median = cv2.medianBlur(img, 21)

# threshold on the white color of cards 
low = (150,150,150)
high = (200,200,200)
thresh = cv2.inRange(median, low, high)

# apply morphology close to remove black regions inside the cards that touch the border
kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT , (31,31))
morph = cv2.morphologyEx(thresh, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)

# get external contours
contours = cv2.findContours(morph, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]

cntr_img = img.copy()
i = 1
for c in contours:
    # get area of contour and filter out small contours
    area = cv2.contourArea(c)
    if area < 5000:
        continue
    
    # get bounding box of contour then
    # filter out horizontal regions as the cards are more vertical than horizontal
    x,y,w,h = cv2.boundingRect(c)
    aspect = h/w
    if aspect < 1:
        continue
        
    # draw contours on copy of input
    cv2.drawContours(cntr_img,[c],0,(255,0,0),4)
    
# save images
thresh_img_file = name + "_thresh.jpg"
morph_img_file = name + "_morph.jpg"
contours_img_file = name + "_contours.jpg"
print(thresh_img_file)
print(morph_img_file)
print(contours_img_file)
cv2.imwrite(thresh_img_file, thresh)
cv2.imwrite(morph_img_file, morph)
cv2.imwrite(contours_img_file, cntr_img)

# show images
cv2.imshow('thresh', thresh)
cv2.imshow('morph', morph)
cv2.imshow('contours', cntr_img)
cv2.waitKey(0)

Q: A process I launched with CreateProcess exited with a code of STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND. How to programmatically detect which DLL was not found? A:

Unfortunately, there is no API for determining the missing library. Your only option would be to manually access and enumerate the executable's IMPORTS table to find out what DLLs it uses, and then recursively access and enumerate their IMPORTS tables, manually checking every DLL reference you find to see whether that DLL file exists on the OS's search path or not.

Q: Set Quarto chunk options such as fig-height from an R object or expression A:

Use !expr in Quarto chunk options to provide values from your environment as options. This way you can calculate the height based on your data, and pass the value to the fig-height option. You need to render the Quarto document to see the resulting height.

Here is a reproducible example:

---
title: "Plot height test"
format: 
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---

With parametrized Quarto reports, certain figures are expected to grow or shrink in widht/height based on existing data. This Quarto report demonstrates how to automatically adjust figure height based on the number of rows present in data. A horizontal column plot (where Y values are groups and X values are a continuous variable, so that bars grow sideways) of fixed height would simply shrink all columns to make them fit in the default height, but in this example, the plot height itself will increase according to the number of rows, so that all plots will have roughly the same column widths.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)

rows <- 23

Data will have {r} rows rows.

data <- data.frame(
  group = letters[1:rows],
  values = sample(10:90, rows, replace = TRUE)
)

base <- 0.3
height <- base * nrow(data)

Based on {r} nrow(data) rows, with a base height of {r} base per row, plot height will be {r} height.

#| fig-height: !expr height
#| fig-width: 5
data |> 
  ggplot() +
  aes(values, group) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_classic()
